column18: Mats of this low-growing shrub are scattered around the cemetery. It seems to survive well under a mowing regime since it never gets very tall.  Astroloma humifusum, with the same growth habit, is also present (see here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/93552887).  Neither were in flower, but I think I have my eye in for the differences now.  Acrotriche has densely white-hairy stems and the leaves at right angles to the stems as in the first photo. Astroloma has less hairy stems on which the red-brown ground colour shows through the hairs, and at least the newer leaves are appressed to the stem.  I compared photos from here of both species to photos I've previously taken which included flowers for confirmation of the ID, and the current photos match well to each species.

column18: In the Flora of Victoria this keys to L. meridionalis, due to its very hairy leaf margins, but not having thought to measure its anthers, I can't get to variety (meridionalis or densiflora).  I assumed in the field that it was L flaccida (or meridionalis var flaccida in the Vic Flora treatment), but it has sparser marginal hairs on the leaves (confirmed by checking some photos from my place of flaccida).  The Aust Virtual Herbarium website has few records of meridionalis from the far south coast, and two of them are also in AVH as flaccida, with identical collection details, so it seems like those IDs are in doubt.  Next time I'll collect a specimen, if I can find it again.

column18: A couple of small clumps of this tiny plant present in the cemetery.  Plants are always very small, so these ones are not dwarfed by regular mowing as many of the plants in the cemetery are; it should be capable of surviving here despite the mowing. It is listed as endangered in NSW, on the basis of there originally being only a single record from 1954 in the Wonboyn area ("on black peaty soil" so probably not in the cemetery).  It's actually not uncommon across southern Australia but only just makes it into SE NSW.  From about 2006 I started finding it in many locations in heath and heathy forest south from about Pambula, so it appears reasonably secure in the area.  It appreciates the freedom from competition from larger plants created by disturbance such as fire and roadworks, sometimes appearing on road verges and in drains in forested country.

A new mistletoe species for me, since we don't have casuarinas on our property. The host is a casuarina beside the river in Tamworth. Host tree shown in the final photo; has a lot of these mistletoes in it. 
Not a difficult ID, but for practise:
Drooping/pendulous habit. Attachment is by a single haustorium forming the terminus of the branch. 
Flowers fully opened all the way to the base of the corolla, therefore Amyema or Diplatia, but neither Diplatia species has the needle-shaped leaves, and there are no bracts around the flowers of the present specimen. Flower buds in axillary umbels of 3-4 rays bearing triads with lateral pair pedunculated and central flower sessile. Buds are quite furry. Leaves are 10-12cm long and needle-shaped.

Second of two mistletoes on separate sub-branches of a branch that had recently fallen from a red gum (not certain of precise host species) beside the river, I guess only a few hours before I came along. Last photo shows where the branch broke off the host. Though I looked with binoculars for more mistletoes in the host tree, I couldn't see any, which I thought was interesting. The immediate neighbouring tree is hosting an A. pendula as well. 
This mistletoe had very long leaves. I took a photo of one against my arm for scale that I estimate was at least 30cm long. No tomentum to notice on leaves or flower buds. Quite a few open flowers, fully open to the base of the corolla, bright orange. Also many buds at fairly advanced stages of development. Umbels with mostly triads, lateral buds pedicelated and central sessile. A few tetrads as well, which had three buds on pedicels arranged at 120° angles and a sessile bud at the centre.

Slashed about twice a year over about 3 years and the sedges increased dramatically in that time.

column18: 6 teeth
When viewed in hand-lens, seeds had white lines along them.

There is a small chance this is a cultivated plant. It was growing amongst mass-planted commonly cultivated native species which had been planted around trees in a park. 

On balance however, I think it is much more likely to be a natural occurrence rather than cultivated - this is because there was only one individual plant (the obvious plantings all had 20+ individuals clearly installed in the area), and that this plant seemed younger than the obvious plantings, and that it is a very uncommon species in cultivation (in my experience as someone whose done plant brokerage work in the preceding years.)

All up I think it is more likely this is a wild one which came up following soil disturbance associated with the plantings. I've seen this species come up following soil disturbance associated with plantings in another garden in the Illawarra (and for that one I was the person doing planting and digging, so I know it comes up naturally in this context).

A diversity of boggy forbs and rushes grew here previously, but most seems to have been sprayed out. Places where there is soil disturbance from kids doing burnouts on e-bikes in the mud seem to be the situation most species are seen regrowing in. If native I hope it makes it to seed before the herbicide is reapplied.
